answer.exemplar: The trick is that the name is not a label for the file, it is the key the bytes are filed under, and a key that changes whenever the content changes turns a cache into something that cannot be wrong. Without the hash, a year-long lifetime is a promise the server has no way to keep for an unnamed file, because the name would be the same whether the file had been corrected or not, and every reader holding a fresh copy would keep it for the whole year. With the hash, a correction produces a different name, a different name is a key nobody holds, and the fetch is therefore guaranteed rather than likely. The arrangement has a shape, though, and the shape is where it stops working. The document that names the hashed files cannot be given the same treatment, because its job is to name the files and a document kept for a year keeps naming the ones it was built with, so the page is right and the content is old. It also assumes the build computes the hash honestly, so a pipeline that republishes a changed file under its old name has quietly reverted the guarantee while keeping the appearance of it, which is the failure that costs a release its fix. And it assumes the file's contents are what matter, so anything outside them, a configuration value baked in at build time under a name that never changed, is not covered by the promise at all.

answer.exemplar: The split exists because the two kinds of request are not equally trustworthy, and the difference comes down to who could have made it. A link, an image and a form all put a request on the wire with no script on the page taking part, and a service receiving one of those cannot tell it apart from a page deliberately reaching for its data, nor refuse it afterwards, because it has already left and may already have changed something on the far side. So for anything a script alone would do, the browser first asks the service a question naming the origin, the method and the headers, and it sends nothing further unless the answer permits them. That relocates the decision to a point where refusing is free, which is the protection the far side is getting: it can set a policy once, in one place, and be sure that nothing arrives that it has not agreed to, rather than discovering afterwards that a request it could not read had already changed its state. The other half of the design is what makes this safe to allow at all, and it is the half that is easy to forget. A simple cross-origin request still gives the page no readable answer unless the service also grants it, so the shape that needs no permission is also the shape that cannot be used to read another origin's data. What remains possible is the side effect, which is a different problem with a different answer, and a service that cares about it has to protect itself with something a cross-origin form cannot supply.
